summary: Phase 1 complete: file-size heuristics derived from web research, adversarially verified
body:
Four parallel researchers (source code, documentation, tests, agent-context files) produced sourced threshold claims; a per-class adversarial verifier fetched each cited URL and killed claims that were unsourced, circular, tool-defaults-passed-off-as-findings, or opinion labelled as measurement. 71 of 85 claims survived; documentation was hit hardest (9 of 25 killed). A synthesizer reconciled survivors into one table, calibrated against this repo's own size distribution. TRADE-OFF MADE: I optimised the HARD thresholds for a reviewable queue and let the SOFT thresholds run noisier. At the values above, hard flags 18 files out of 1,450 tracked (1.2%) and soft flags roughly 61 (4.2%). Rejected alternatives and why: a flat 300 LOC -- the ESLint/Airbnb reference value and the single most commonly cited number -- yields 319 violators here, which is a rename of 'most files' and cannot function as a heuristic; note ESLint ships it OFF and Airbnb writes it as ['off', {max:300}], so neither actually enforces it. A flat 500 yields 115, still an unworkable backlog. A flat 1000 yields 25, close to workable but wrong in shape: it lets ts-src/index.ts (1300) through while it would flag nothing at all in py-src or shell, where the local distributions make 878 and 806 the genuine outliers.

SO I SET THRESHOLDS PER CLASS, WHICH IS ITSELF DEFENSIBLE FROM THE LITERATURE, NOT JUST FROM CONVENIENCE: Herraiz's fitted outlier points differ by language on measured data (Python 826, C++ 1258, C 1820 SLOC), and SonarSource ships the same rule id at 750 for Java and 1000 for JS/TS. Where a citation and the repo distribution agreed I used the citation (rust-src hard 2000 = Checkstyle; py-src hard 800 ~= Herraiz's Python 826; py-test hard 1000 = Sonar S104 Python; ts-src hard 1000 = SonarJS S104; design-doc and plan-status-doc = Wikipedia word rows converted at this repo's measured 8.3 words/line; agent-file = Anthropic's stated 200-line target plus the 5,000-token post-compaction cap converted at 14.7 tokens/line). Where no citation exists for the class I said so in the rationale rather than dressing a percentile up as sourced: py-eval hard, rust-test soft and hard, py-test soft, ts-test hard, shell soft and hard, and shell-test hard are all repo-calibration judgments, generally set at ~1.5-2x the class p95 so they flag files that are outliers WITHIN THEIR OWN CLASS.

WHAT THIS COSTS: hard thresholds tuned to flag ~1% mean the table is nearly silent on files that are merely large-and-awkward. src/rust/crates/fathomdb-cli/src/lib.rs (1050) and fathomdb-schema/src/lib.rs (999) sit just under rust-src's hard line and are soft-only or invisible; six plan-status docs over 1,000 lines draw no verdict at all. That is the deliberate trade: I would rather have 18 findings a reviewer actually adjudicates than 115 that get bulk-waived, which is how a size gate dies. The soft tier absorbs the rest as advisory.

WHAT THE TABLE WOULD FLAG, IN PRIORITY ORDER: src/rust/crates/fathomdb-engine/src/lib.rs at 17,910 lines is in a category of its own -- 6x rustc tidy's own hard build-failing limit, 9x Checkstyle's tripwire, 17x Herraiz's empirical outlier point, and ~2.5x the next-largest file class-normalised. If only one finding survives triage, it is that one. Then the two FFI shims (2678, 2561), then the three doc hard-hits (of which two should be excluded as archived/locked), then the singletons per class. agent-file returns clean at 0/11 as predicted -- but see the disagreements: a clean per-file agent row says nothing about the aggregate always-loaded budget, which is where this repo's actual context pressure lives (a 2,087-line STATUS file read mid-session is ~32k tokens, larger than the whole post-compaction skill pool).

UNIT: Native unit. Raw physical lines (`wc -l`) on tracked .rs files, matching how the repo counts were produced. Sonar S104 and Yamashita measure LOC-excluding-blanks/comments; this repo's Rust files average 4.46 words/line, so physical-line counts run roughly 20-30% above a blanks/comments-stripped count. Both thresholds are therefore slightly LOOSER in effect than the cited numbers.

RATIONALE: Soft 1000 is the convergence point of three independent tool defaults (pylint max-module-lines 1000, SonarJS S104 1000, PMD ExcessiveClassLength 1000) and sits essentially on Herraiz's data-derived lognormal->power-law transition of 1,072 SLOC across 1.36M Debian files -- the closest thing in the literature to an empirical 'this file is now an outlier' line. Yamashita's 90th-percentile 'very high risk' band (847-975 LOC) brackets the same place. Hard 2000 is Checkstyle's FileLength default, explicitly framed as a last-resort 'this file has clearly gone wrong' tripwire rather than a design target -- exactly the semantics wanted for a hard verdict. I did NOT use rustc tidy's 3000 as the hard line even though it is the only real per-file Rust limit shipped anywhere, because at 3000 this repo yields exactly one violator and the two FFI shims (2678, 2561) escape review; tidy's 3000 is recorded here as the ceiling above which the file is indefensible under ANY published rule. Repo effect: soft flags 4/27, hard flags 3/27 (engine/src/lib.rs 17910, py/src/lib.rs 2678, napi/src/lib.rs 2561). engine/src/lib.rs is 6x rustc's own hard limit and 17x the empirical outlier line -- it is the single most anomalous file in the repo by a wide margin.

CITATIONS:
  - https://checkstyle.sourceforge.io/checks/sizes/filelength.html -- FileLength max=2000, last-resort tripwire (HARD basis)
  - https://www.scitepress.org/Papers/2011/34262/34262.pdf -- Herraiz et al., Debian 5.0.2, 1,355,752 files: power-law transition x_min = 1,072 SLOC (SOFT basis)
  - https://github.com/pylint-dev/pylint/blob/main/pylint/checkers/format.py -- max-module-lines default 1000
  - https://github.com/SonarSource/SonarJS/blob/master/packages/analysis/src/jsts/rules/S104/config.ts -- S104 maximum default 1000
  - https://posl.ait.kyushu-u.ac.jp/~kamei/publications/Yamashita_QRS2016.pdf -- 90th-percentile 'very high risk' 847-975 LOC over 1,000 Java projects
  - https://github.com/rust-lang/rust/blob/master/src/tools/tidy/src/style.rs -- rustc tidy const LINES = 3000, hard build failure (context: the only shipped Rust per-file limit)
  - https://github.com/rust-lang/rust-clippy/blob/master/clippy_config/src/conf.rs -- clippy has NO file-level line lint; too_many_lines_threshold=100 regulates functions only

UNIT: Native unit, raw physical lines. No conversion. The literature offers no test-FILE line threshold for Rust at all; the only test-file-specific line number found anywhere was sass-spec's 500-line HRX guidance, which is not language-comparable.

RATIONALE: Deliberately looser than rust-src at the soft end is NOT what I did -- I set soft TIGHTER (800 vs 1000) and hard tighter (1200 vs 2000), and that is a repo-calibration judgment, not a literature finding. Reasoning: the class is large (164 files, p95=826) and tightly distributed, so 800 is its own p95, whereas rust-src is 27 files with a pathological tail. The literature actually cuts the other way and I am overriding it: Checkstyle's file-length rationale is comprehension-of-one-cohesive-class, which maps poorly onto a file of N independent #[test] functions; rubocop-rspec, the only purpose-built test linter examined, ships NO spec-file-length cop at all and regulates per-example size (Max 5 lines) and nesting depth (Max 3) instead. The measured test-smell work (Spadini et al., 1,489 projects, 25.4 MLOC) also derives every threshold per test METHOD (30 statements = very-high 'Long Test'), never per file. So treat a rust-test hard hit as a prompt to check per-test size and setup duplication first, and only then to split the file. Repo effect: soft ~9/164, hard 2/164 (perf_gates.rs 1581, slice15d_projection_registry.rs 1277).

CITATIONS:
  - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rubocop/rubocop-rspec/master/config/default.yml -- no spec-file-length cop exists; RSpec/ExampleLength Max 5, RSpec/NestedGroups Max 3 (basis for regulating per-test, not per-file)
  - https://sback.it/publications/msr2020.pdf -- Spadini et al., benchmark-derived thresholds over 1,489 projects: 'Long Test' very-high at 30 statements PER METHOD
  - https://checkstyle.sourceforge.io/checks/sizes/filelength.html -- 2000, with the class-comprehension rationale that does not transfer to test files
  - https://posl.ait.kyushu-u.ac.jp/~kamei/publications/Yamashita_QRS2016.pdf -- 90th-percentile 847-975 LOC (nearest empirical anchor; 800 sits just below it)
  - REPO-CALIBRATION: soft 800 = class p95 (826); hard 1200 = ~1.5x p95, chosen to flag exactly the two files that stand outside the class distribution

UNIT: Native unit, raw physical lines. Herraiz's Python figure is SLOC (826); this repo's Python averages 4.19 words/line, so 800 physical lines is somewhat fewer than 800 SLOC -- the hard threshold is therefore modestly tighter than the cited 826, which I accepted rather than rounding up.

RATIONALE: Hard 800 rounds down from Herraiz's language-specific fitted power-law transition for Python, x_min = 826 SLOC over 63,590 .py files (median 59) -- notably tighter than C's 1,820 and C++'s 1,258, which is direct evidence that a flat cross-language number is wrong and that pylint's 1000 is too loose for Python specifically. Soft 500 is Clean Code's observed ceiling ('none exceeds 500 lines' across Junit/Fitnesse/Time-and-Money); I use it as an advisory only and flag it as weak evidence -- it is an argument from three hand-picked codebases with no outcome measure, and it is the origin of the folk '500-line rule'. pylint's own 1000 default would flag ZERO files in this class and is useless here. Repo effect: soft 4/50, hard 1/50 (dev/agent-tools/ledgerwatch/ledgerwatch.py 878).

CITATIONS:
  - https://www.scitepress.org/Papers/2011/34262/34262.pdf -- Python-specific x_min = 826 SLOC, median 59 (HARD basis; language-specific, measured)
  - https://github.com/azizkayumov/clean-code/blob/main/formatting.md -- Clean Code ch.5: most files <200 lines, none exceeds 500 (SOFT basis; evidence_strength = argued, three codebases, no outcome measure)
  - https://github.com/pylint-dev/pylint/blob/main/pylint/checkers/format.py -- max-module-lines 1000 (rejected as too loose for this class: zero repo violators)

UNIT: Native unit, raw physical lines. No conversion.

RATIONALE: REPO-CALIBRATION JUDGMENT with only partial literature backing. There is no published threshold for single-shot experiment/eval scripts anywhere in the surviving evidence. This class is structurally different from py-src: median 368 lines vs 133, p90 873 vs 322 -- these are run-once analysis pipelines whose value is reproducibility of a specific experiment, not long-term maintainability, and splitting them fragments the record of what was actually run. Soft 800 borrows Herraiz's Python transition (826) as the nearest empirical anchor but is applied here as advisory only. Hard 1200 has NO literature backing: it is 1.5x the class p90 and was chosen to flag only the two scripts that stand clearly outside their own class. El Emam's finding that there is no threshold effect of size on defects is especially applicable here -- for throwaway eval code, a split is pure churn with no predicted defect benefit. Repo effect: soft ~6/56, hard 2/56 (s15a_embedder_probe.py 1562, r2_parity_eval.py 1494).

CITATIONS:
  - https://www.scitepress.org/Papers/2011/34262/34262.pdf -- Python x_min = 826 SLOC (SOFT anchor only)
  - https://nrc-publications.canada.ca/eng/view/ft/?id=e709a57a-b4b9-4e73-83e2-4adb489a9836 -- El Emam et al.: 'unambiguous evidence that there is no threshold effect of class size' (basis for treating this class leniently)
  - REPO-CALIBRATION: hard 1200 = ~1.4x class p90 (873); no literature number exists for eval/experiment scripts

UNIT: Native unit, raw physical lines. Sonar S104's Python variant counts lines of code excluding blanks/comments; at 4.19 words/line here, 1000 physical lines is meaningfully fewer than 1000 Sonar-LOC, so the hard threshold is tighter in effect than the citation.

RATIONALE: Hard 1000 is Sonar's rule S104 for Python, whose metadata sets scope='All' -- Sonar has an explicit main-vs-test scoping mechanism (scope='Tests', used for S2699) and deliberately did NOT scope the file-length rule to main sources, so applying it to test files is a positive vendor decision rather than an oversight. pylint's max-module-lines 1000 has no test-path carve-out either, giving two independent tools at the same number. Soft 600 is a REPO-CALIBRATION judgment (class p95 = 607) with no literature backing; the cited test-linter evidence (rubocop-rspec) declines to set any spec-file threshold at all, so a soft line here is a local convention. Repo effect: soft 7/128, hard 1/128 (dev/agent-tools/ledgerwatch/test_ledgerwatch.py 1061).

CITATIONS:
  - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/SonarSource/sonar-python/master/python-checks/src/main/java/org/sonar/python/checks/TooManyLinesInFileCheck.java -- S104 Python, 1000, scope='All' i.e. tests explicitly in scope (HARD basis)
  - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/pylint-dev/pylint/main/pylint/checkers/format.py -- max-module-lines 1000, no test carve-out
  - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rubocop/rubocop-rspec/master/config/default.yml -- purpose-built test linter with NO file-length cop (why soft is local convention, not literature)
  - REPO-CALIBRATION: soft 600 = class p95 (607)

UNIT: Native unit, raw physical lines. SonarJS S104 counts 'lines in a file'; ESLint max-lines defaults to counting all lines unless skipBlankLines/skipComments are set (Airbnb sets both). No conversion applied.

RATIONALE: Hard 1000 is SonarJS's own S104 default for JS/TS -- notable because SonarSource sets the SAME rule id 33% looser for JS/TS than for Java (750), which is itself evidence the numbers are conventions rather than measured breakpoints. Soft 500 is Clean Code's observed ceiling, used advisory-only. I explicitly REJECTED ESLint's 300 and Airbnb's 300 as thresholds: ESLint ships max-lines off by default, Airbnb writes it as ['off', { max: 300 }] -- a style guide documenting a number while declining to enforce it -- and applying 300 across this repo yields 319 violators, which is a rename of 'most files', not a heuristic. Class is tiny (6 files), so percentile calibration is meaningless; the thresholds are pure literature here. Repo effect: soft 2/6 (index.ts 1300, binding.ts 518), hard 1/6 (src/ts/src/index.ts 1300).

CITATIONS:
  - https://github.com/SonarSource/SonarJS/blob/master/packages/analysis/src/jsts/rules/S104/config.ts -- JS/TS maximum default 1000 (HARD basis)
  - https://github.com/azizkayumov/clean-code/blob/main/formatting.md -- 500-line observed ceiling (SOFT basis, argued not measured)
  - https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/max-lines -- max:300 reference value, rule OFF unless enabled (rejected)
  - https://github.com/airbnb/javascript/blob/master/packages/eslint-config-airbnb-base/rules/style.js -- 'max-lines': ['off', { max: 300 }] -- documented but deliberately unenforced (rejected)

UNIT: Native unit, raw physical lines. sass-spec's 500 is stated as raw lines of an HRX file, so no conversion.

RATIONALE: Soft 500 is the ONLY test-file-specific line threshold found in any real project style guide: sass-spec's "DON'T have HRX files longer than 500 lines or so", and it usefully names the counter-risk in the same breath -- splitting can create 'too many small files', in which case you recombine. Hard 750 is a REPO-CALIBRATION judgment with no literature backing (class p95 = 383, so 750 is ~2x p95); SonarJS's 1000 would flag zero files in this class. ESLint's max-lines-per-function (default 50) is the rule that would actually bite these files, since a whole suite wrapped in one describe() is a single enormous function -- worth noting as the more diagnostic signal than file length. Repo effect: soft 2/42, hard 1/42 (src/ts/tests/slice10-read-view.test.ts 755).

CITATIONS:
  - https://github.com/sass/sass-spec/blob/master/STYLE_GUIDE.md -- 'DON'T have HRX files longer than 500 lines or so', plus the explicit recombine counter-rule (SOFT basis)
  - https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/max-lines-per-function -- default 50; the describe() wrapper makes this the rule that actually fires on test files
  - https://eslint.org/docs/latest/rules/max-lines -- no default exemption for *.test.* / *.spec.*; any test carve-out is a team config choice
  - REPO-CALIBRATION: hard 750 = ~2x class p95 (383); SonarJS 1000 would flag zero files here

UNIT: Native unit, raw physical lines. Google's shell guide states its limit in plain lines, so no conversion.

RATIONALE: BOTH numbers are REPO-CALIBRATION judgments that knowingly diverge from the one applicable citation. Google's Shell Style Guide gives a genuine, rare, explicit per-file limit: a script 'more than 100 lines long, or that uses non-straightforward control flow logic' should be rewritten in a structured language NOW. Applied literally to this repo that flags ~22 of 62 shell files (class p70 = 121), which is not actionable -- the repo has made a standing choice to write substantial governance/CI tooling in bash. So soft 200 (~class p80) and hard 500 are local conventions; Google's 100 is retained as the literature value and the divergence is recorded in disagreements rather than hidden by picking a comfortable number and calling it sourced. Note Google's second clause -- non-straightforward control flow -- is arguably the better trigger and is not length-based at all. Repo effect: soft 10/62, hard 1/62 (scripts/commission-manifest.sh 806, which is 8x Google's rewrite trigger and the strongest 'port this to Python' candidate in the repo).

CITATIONS:
  - https://google.github.io/styleguide/shellguide.html -- 'more than 100 lines long, or that uses non-straightforward control flow logic' => rewrite in a structured language (the only literature number for this class; repo diverges deliberately)
  - REPO-CALIBRATION: soft 200 = ~class p80 (174-278 band); hard 500 = 5x Google's trigger, chosen to flag exactly the one script that is an outlier within its own class

UNIT: Native unit, raw physical lines. No conversion.

RATIONALE: Soft 500 reuses the sass-spec test-file guidance (the only test-scoped file-length number in the evidence set), applied cross-language, which is a stretch and is marked as such. Hard 800 is a REPO-CALIBRATION judgment with no literature backing: class p95 = 645, so 800 flags only the single script above its own distribution. Google's shell 100-line rule is not applied to this class at all -- these are bats-style harnesses of many independent assertions, and the same argument that defeats file-length rules for test code (rubocop-rspec ships no spec-file cop; Spadini's measured thresholds are all per test method) applies. A shell-test hard hit should first be checked for copy-pasted setup blocks, not split by line count. Repo effect: soft 4/33, hard 1/33 (scripts/tests/test_commission_manifest.sh 882 -- note it tests the 806-line script that is itself the shell class's only hard violator).

CITATIONS:
  - https://github.com/sass/sass-spec/blob/master/STYLE_GUIDE.md -- 500-line test-file guidance (SOFT basis, cross-language application is a stretch)
  - https://raw.githubusercontent.com/rubocop/rubocop-rspec/master/config/default.yml -- no test-file length cop; per-example and nesting-depth limits instead
  - https://sback.it/publications/msr2020.pdf -- measured test-smell thresholds are all per test method, never per file
  - REPO-CALIBRATION: hard 800 = just above class p95 (645)

UNIT: CONVERTED FROM WORDS. Wikipedia states its thresholds in readable-prose words. Measured on this repo's 882 tracked .md files: 8.35 words per physical line (163,919 lines, blank lines included); design/*.md specifically is 8.79 words/line. Using 8.35: 6,000 words = 719 lines -> soft 700; 9,000 words = 1,078 lines -> hard 1100; 15,000 words = 1,796 lines. CAVEAT that cuts against me: Wikipedia's 'readable prose' explicitly EXCLUDES tables, lists, code blocks and references, and this repo's docs are heavily list/table/code-dense, so a 700-line doc here contains materially fewer than 6,000 prose words. Both thresholds are therefore TIGHTER in prose terms than the citations they derive from -- I accepted that rather than inflating the line numbers, because the excluded material still costs a reader (and an agent's context) real tokens.

RATIONALE: Soft 700 is Wikipedia's explicit safe-harbour boundary: below 6,000 words 'length alone does not justify division or trimming', and that boundary is backed by a measured distribution (98.5% of all articles and 76% of Featured articles fall below it). Hard 1100 is the 9,000-word row: 'probably should be divided or trimmed, though the scope of a topic can sometimes justify the added reading material' -- a rebuttable presumption, which is exactly the right strength for 'needs a verdict'. I did not use the 15,000-word row (1,800 lines) as the hard line for this class because it would flag zero design docs. Two non-length signals from MDN are better triggers than either number and should be checked alongside: needing a fourth heading level means the page holds more than one topic, and MDN sets a MINIMUM (~300 words) because over-short pages are hard to find -- splitting has a real discoverability cost, so 'split it' is not free. Repo effect: soft ~10/405, hard 3/405 (performance-whitepaper-notes.md 1665, dev/acceptance.md 1305, dev/archive/hitl-queue.md 1151 -- and two of those three should be excluded by rule, see exclusion_rules).

CITATIONS:
  - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Article_size -- '> 6,000 words: length alone does not justify division or trimming' (98.5% of articles below); '> 9,000 words: probably should be divided or trimmed' (SOFT and HARD bases)
  - https://developer.mozilla.org/en-US/docs/MDN/Writing_guidelines/Writing_style_guide -- 'not more than three levels of headers... consider breaking up the article'; and a ~300-word MINIMUM because short pages are hard to find
  - https://www.nngroup.com/articles/how-little-do-users-read/ -- Nielsen: users read half the content only at <=111 words (context: any doc page well past ~13 lines is mostly skimmed, which argues for navigability over splitting)
  - https://learn.microsoft.com/en-us/style-guide/scannable-content/ -- prescribes TOC + 'Back to top' for long docs, i.e. NAVIGATE rather than split

UNIT: CONVERTED FROM WORDS, same basis as design-doc. Measured 8.21 words/line across this repo's 448 plan/progress/STATUS markdown files. 9,000 words = 1,096 lines -> soft 1100; 15,000 words = 1,827 lines -> hard 1800. Same prose-exclusion caveat applies, and it bites harder here: STATUS files are almost entirely tables, checklists and commit shas, so their readable-prose word count is far below 8.21/line.

RATIONALE: DELIBERATELY TREATED DIFFERENTLY FROM design-doc, and the evidence supports it. Keep a Changelog 2.0.0 is the strongest single item in the whole evidence set on this point: it sets NO length limit at all -- 'a single file is usually fine, even a long one; many projects keep decades of history in one CHANGELOG.md', split only when it 'becomes hard to manage', and 'do not delete old entries'. Growth is the expected steady state for an append-only record, not a defect. Concretely: the line at which a design-doc gets a HARD verdict (1100) is only ADVISORY here, and the hard line is pushed out to Wikipedia's most permissive row, 15,000 words / 'almost certainly should be divided or trimmed'. Splitting a STATUS file also destroys the property that makes it useful -- a single chronological spine you can bisect against git history. The correct response to a hard hit is Keep a Changelog's own prescription (move OLD history to an archive file, link both ways), never a topical split. ONE HONEST COUNTERWEIGHT: Keep a Changelog assumes a human reader who greps; these STATUS files are read by agents mid-session, so they also draw on the context budget that the agent-file row governs -- a 2,087-line STATUS is ~32k tokens at this repo's ~15.5 tokens/line, larger than the entire 25k-token post-compaction skill pool. That cost is real and is not addressed by any documentation citation. Repo effect: soft 3/466, hard 1/466 (dev/plans/runs/STATUS-0.8.0.md 2087).

CITATIONS:
  - https://keepachangelog.com/en/2.0.0/ -- 'A single file is usually fine, even a long one'; split only 'if it becomes hard to manage', archive old history and link both ways; 'do not delete old entries' (basis for the whole lenient treatment)
  - https://en.wikipedia.org/wiki/Wikipedia:Article_size -- '> 9,000 words: probably should be divided' (SOFT); '> 15,000 words: almost certainly should be divided or trimmed' (HARD)
  - https://cognitect.com/blog/2011/11/15/documenting-architecture-decisions -- ADRs are one-to-two pages and superseded records are KEPT and marked, not deleted (supports append-only history as correct practice; note 'pages' is an unstable unit for Markdown and is not used numerically here)
  - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills -- 25,000-token combined post-compaction budget (the counterweight: agent-read status files are not free)

UNIT: MIXED UNITS, conversion shown. The soft number is native: Claude Code's memory docs state 'target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file' in lines, and the MEMORY.md index is HARD-truncated at 200 lines (or 25 KB, whichever first). The hard number is CONVERTED FROM TOKENS: Claude Code re-attaches only the first 5,000 tokens of each invoked skill after auto-compaction. Measured on this repo's 11 agent files: 58.9 chars/line and 8.30 words/line. OpenAI's published ratio (~4 chars/token, ~0.75 words/token) is the only vendor conversion available and it is character/word based -- NO vendor publishes a lines-to-tokens conversion. That gives 14.7 tokens/line (chars/4) or 11.1 tokens/line (words/0.75); I use the conservative 14.7. 5,000 tokens / 14.7 = 340 lines -> hard 350. Corollary worth stating: the 200-line soft target is ~2,900-3,000 tokens, which lands almost exactly on the measured degradation points below -- the vendor guidance and the empirical literature agree by coincidence of units.

RATIONALE: Soft 200 is verbatim vendor guidance with a stated mechanism ('Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence'), and it is independently corroborated by measurement: Liu et al. found a 22.0-point positional penalty at avg 2,946 input tokens (GPT-3.5-Turbo 75.8% at position 1 vs 53.8% mid-context -- below its 56.1% CLOSED-BOOK score, i.e. the context actively hurt), and Levy et al. found accuracy falling 0.92 -> 0.68 when only irrelevant padding grew to 3,000 tokens. Both sit at ~200 lines of this repo's markdown. Hard 350 is the durability line: past ~5,000 tokens, instruction content is not re-attached after compaction, so it silently stops governing behaviour in exactly the long sessions where governance matters most. Anthropic's SKILL.md guidance of 500 lines is the looser sibling and is justified by on-demand rather than every-session loading -- if a file in this class is genuinely a SKILL.md body, 500 is the right soft line, not 200. AS PREDICTED, THIS CLASS COMES BACK CLEAN: max 159 lines (.claude/agents/steward.md), 0 soft and 0 hard violators across 11 files. The binding constraint in this repo is not any individual agent file; it is aggregate always-loaded context, which no per-file threshold measures -- OpenAI Codex caps the whole AGENTS.md chain at 32,768 bytes, and Claude Code caps the skill listing at 1% of the context window and the post-compaction skill pool at 25,000 tokens. A per-file table cannot see those, and a green agent-file row is not evidence that the aggregate budget is healthy.

CITATIONS:
  - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/memory -- 'Size: target under 200 lines per CLAUDE.md file. Longer files consume more context and reduce adherence.' (SOFT); MEMORY.md index hard-truncated at 200 lines / 25 KB
  - https://code.claude.com/docs/en/skills -- only the first 5,000 tokens of each invoked skill are re-attached after auto-compaction; 25,000-token combined pool, most-recent-first; listing capped at 1% of context window (HARD basis)
  - https://platform.claude.com/docs/en/agents-and-tools/agent-skills/best-practices -- 'Keep SKILL.md body under 500 lines for optimal performance'; description field hard-capped at 1,024 chars
  - https://developers.openai.com/api/docs/concepts -- '1 token is approximately 4 characters or 0.75 words for English text' (the ONLY published conversion, and it is not line-based)
  - https://arxiv.org/pdf/2307.03172v3 -- Liu et al.: 22.0-point mid-context penalty at avg 2,946 tokens; 15.6 points already at avg 1,476 tokens

summary: THE DEFECT RESEARCH ARGUES AGAINST SPLITTING, AND THIS TABLE DOES NOT REST ON A DEFECT CLAIM
body: THE DEFECT RESEARCH ARGUES AGAINST SPLITTING, AND THIS TABLE DOES NOT REST ON A DEFECT CLAIM. El Emam et al. showed the U-shaped 'optimal component size' result is a MATHEMATICAL ARTIFACT of regressing defects/LOC against LOC, then tested threshold models directly on three systems with four size measures and reported 'unambiguous evidence that there is no threshold effect of class size'. Yamashita et al. add that although larger files are more likely to contain at least one defect, their defect DENSITY is monotonically LOWER. Taken together: there is no cliff to defend, and splitting a 1,200-line file into four 300-line files has no predicted defect benefit. Every hard threshold above is therefore an ATTENTION-ALLOCATION device (where should a reviewer look first, and what costs an agent the most context) -- not a claim that the file is buggy or that splitting it will make it less buggy. Anyone citing this table as 'large file = defect risk' is misciting the literature.

summary: HATTON POINTS THE OPPOSITE WAY BELOW ~200 LINES
body: HATTON POINTS THE OPPOSITE WAY BELOW ~200 LINES. Hatton's model predicts components get proportionally WORSE, not better, below a short-term-memory cutoff 'in the region of 200-400 lines and apparently independent of language'. MDN independently sets a ~300-word MINIMUM for doc pages because short pages are hard to find. So aggressive splitting has a measured downside, and sass-spec names the same failure mode for tests ('too many small HRX files' -> recombine). No lower bound is enforced in this table, but 'fix' should never mean shattering a 900-line file into ten 90-line ones.

summary: THE VENDOR NUMBERS CONTRADICT EACH OTHER AND ARE UNSOURCED
body: THE VENDOR NUMBERS CONTRADICT EACH OTHER AND ARE UNSOURCED. SonarSource ships rule S104 at 750 for Java and 1000 for JS/TS -- same rule id, same vendor, 33% apart, no evidence cited either way. Checkstyle says 2000, ESLint 300 (off by default), rustc tidy 3000, Google's C++ and Java guides set NO file limit at all, and the Linux kernel style guide is silent on .c file length while capping functions at ~48 lines. There is no consensus file-length number in the industry; the consensus is that FUNCTION length is what gets regulated (clippy 100, Google C++ ~40, kernel ~48, ESLint max-lines-per-function 50, Chowdhury et al.'s measured 24 lines for Java methods over ~785K methods). Any per-file table, including this one, is a convention wearing citations.

summary: TEST-FILE THRESHOLDS ARE THE WEAKEST ROWS IN THE TABLE
body: TEST-FILE THRESHOLDS ARE THE WEAKEST ROWS IN THE TABLE. The purpose-built test linter (rubocop-rspec, ~1067 lines of cop config) defines NO spec-file-length cop at all, and the only measured test thresholds in the literature (Spadini et al., 1,489 projects, 25.4 MLOC) are all per test METHOD -- 30 statements, 39 production calls, 10 unmessaged assertions at very-high severity. That same work found the classic Eager Test threshold of 1 was about 39x too strict, i.e. hand-set test thresholds have a documented history of being badly wrong. Counter-evidence exists (Sonar deliberately scopes S104 to 'All', not 'Tests'; ESLint ships no test exemption), so tests are not exempt -- but a rust-test/py-test/ts-test/shell-test hard hit should be investigated per-test first and only split as a second resort.

In this repo, STATUS and plan files are read by agents mid-session, where dev/plans/runs/STATUS-0.8.0.md at 2,087 lines is roughly 32,000 tokens at the measured 15.5 tokens/line -- larger than Claude Code's entire 25,000-token post-compaction skill pool, and an order of magnitude past the ~2-3k token range where Liu et al. and Levy et al. measure real degradation. The documentation literature says leave it alone; the context literature says it is already too big to be read reliably. I resolved this in favour of the documentation literature (hard 1800 lines, one violator) because splitting destroys the chronological spine, but the tension is genuine and the right fix is probably archive-and-link, not a threshold.

Two thresholds were dropped as unconvertible: Copilot's '2 pages' and Nygard's 'one or two pages'.

summary: Nine classes of file are exempt from length thresholds by rule
body:
- GENERATED CODE: anything emitted by a build step or codegen tool (target/, site/, dist/, build/, *.pb.go, *_generated.*, bindings emitted by napi/maturin, mkdocs output). Length is an artifact of the generator, so a threshold measures nothing a human can act on. Note this does NOT exempt hand-written FFI shims -- src/rust/crates/fathomdb-py/src/lib.rs and fathomdb-napi/src/lib.rs are authored code and remain hard violators.

- VENDORED / THIRD-PARTY: node_modules/, any vendor/ or third_party/ tree, git submodules. Not the repo's code to split; a violation is unactionable and re-appears on every upgrade.

- LOCKFILES AND MACHINE-MAINTAINED MANIFESTS: Cargo.lock, package-lock.json, *.lock, dev/perf-history/*.json, dev/plans/release-state-*.json. Content and length are tool-determined; editing them for size is actively harmful.

- GOLDEN / FIXTURE / CORPUS DATA: tests/corpus/**, dev/acceptance-rowsets/**, data/**, any *.golden / *.snap / expected-output file, and eval corpora (LOCOMO, AP-News payloads). Size tracks the size of the phenomenon under test; splitting a golden file breaks the identity between fixture and assertion.

- APPEND-ONLY LEDGERS AND JSONL RECORDS: dev/todos-and-considerations-ledger.jsonl, dev/design/record-lifecycle-protocol/OPP-12-sub-ledger.jsonl, any *.jsonl. These are governed by seq-contiguity, not length; per Keep a Changelog, unbounded growth is the intended steady state and entries are never deleted.

- LOG AND TRANSCRIPT ARTIFACTS: *.log (e.g. dev/plans/runs/codex/**/*.log), captured review transcripts, run outputs. They are evidence records; truncating or splitting them destroys the audit chain they exist to provide.

- ARCHIVED / FROZEN DOCUMENTS: dev/archive/** and superseded records explicitly marked as such. Nygard's ADR practice is to KEEP superseded records and mark them, not to edit them; in this repo that exempts dev/archive/hitl-queue.md (1151) and dev/archive/psd/0.6.0-system-psd.md (1016) from the design-doc hard rule.

- LOCKED SPECIFICATION FILES under an explicit governance freeze -- in this repo, dev/acceptance.md (1305) is recorded as locked with no per-feature ACs. A file that cannot be edited by policy cannot be a length violation; if it must be split, that is a governance decision, not a hygiene finding.

- CHANGELOG.md and any release-history file: exempt by direct citation, not by judgment. Keep a Changelog 2.0.0 states a single long file is fine and old entries must not be deleted.

summary: engine/src/lib.rs decomposes to ~20 modules with ZERO public API change
body:
Enabling fact the whole plan rests on: Rust allows inherent impl blocks for a type to live in ANY module of the defining crate, and private fields are visible in the defining module and all descendants. So struct Engine stays in lib.rs and ~16 capability modules each carry their own 'impl Engine { .. }'. Engine::search() stays Engine::search() for every consumer: no facade, no visibility churn, no API change.

HARD CONSTRAINT: struct Engine must stay in lib.rs. If it is moved into engine/mod.rs with the capability modules as siblings, private-field access breaks everywhere and the plan collapses into a pub(crate)-field rewrite.

The finding that reframed this: impl Engine is 5008 lines / 140 methods, but median method length is 20 lines and only 2 exceed 200. The methods are fine. One TYPE carries 140 responsibilities. So the decomposition is by capability cluster, not by line count.

See dev/plans/refactor-background-check/engine-decomposition.md for the full module tree.

They share patterns (cd to toplevel, tool-presence checks, structured error reporting, exit-code semantics) but NOT code. Each is independently deployable and deliberately self-contained: check-release-state-views, check-governed-surface-pin, and check-ledgers embed Python; lint-plan-anchors embeds Perl; preflight and steward-orient orchestrate multiple checks; set-version manages version axes. The standing rule ("fix tooling so it cannot recur") applies: each script is a specialized gate that precisely documents its own failure mode and remedy, making it independently understandable and auditable. Extracting a common bash library would save 5-10 lines per script at the cost of added complexity and indirection with minimal gain.

summary: Engine decomposition's load-bearing Rust visibility claim CONFIRMED BY COMPILATION, both directions
body:
Not argued - compiled. A throwaway crate (rustc 1.95.0, edition 2021 matching the workspace) with a crate-root struct holding fully private fields plus two sibling capability modules, each writing its own inherent impl block touching a different private field, and one calling the other's method: cargo build exit 0.

The predicted FAILURE mode was also reproduced: moving the struct into a child module while the capability modules stay siblings fails with error[E0616] 'field is private' - the exact error the plan predicts. And the named mitigation was confirmed minimal and sufficient: changing only the two field declarations to pub(crate) makes the identical code compile, which is precisely the 'pub(crate)-field rewrite' the plan says the effort degenerates into.

Obstruction scan of the real crate came back clean: zero macro_rules! anywhere in the crate, zero pyo3/napi proc-macro attrs, struct Engine at L274 with all ~20 fields plain-private, exactly one top-level impl Engine at L4110, and no name collisions between the ~20 planned modules and the existing lifecycle/pcache2/reader_search_hook/mean_centering_internals_for_test modules.

summary: markdownlint --fix corrupts bare leading-underscore identifiers in agent free-text; third occurrence of this class in this repo
body:
Twice in this session, md-safe-fix caught markdownlint --fix merging a bare identifier into the preceding word: "The _fathomdb" -> "The_fathomdb", and "for _fathomdb.pyi" -> "for_fathomdb.pyi". The AST guard worked correctly both times and reverted the change - the guard is not the problem.

The problem is upstream: agent free-text (blast_radius, evidence, why_big fields) routinely contains identifiers like _fathomdb, _lib, __init__, and any generator that renders that text verbatim into markdown emits a construct markdownlint will corrupt. Patching the rendered file fixes one instance and the next generation reintroduces it.

Fixed at the generator: bare leading-underscore identifiers are now backticked before rendering, splitting on existing code spans so already-backticked ones are untouched.

Per the standing rule that guardrail failures are fixed in tooling rather than by asking people to be careful, the durable version of this fix belongs in whatever shared markdown-rendering helper future agent-output-to-markdown pipelines use, not re-implemented per script. Related to the steward ledger seq-95/96 and seq-109 (TC-53) shell-expansion corruption class: same shape - a text transform silently altering meaning between an agent and a file - different mechanism.

summary: HITL RATIFIED: the shell threshold override stands. Google 100-line rule REJECTED for this repo.
body:
Phase 1 flagged this as the single genuinely open calibration decision. The Google Shell Style Guide says a script over 100 lines "should be rewritten in a structured language now"; this repo has ~22 shell files above that, topped by scripts/commission-manifest.sh at 806. The synthesizer set shell to soft 200 / hard 500 as a local convention and explicitly asked that it be made an explicit, revisitable decision rather than a silently-chosen number.

HITL has now ruled: the override stands. Google 100 does not govern this repo.

This CLOSES the item by decision, not by measurement. The threshold is no longer a repo-calibration guess awaiting review - it is a ratified local convention, and the Phase 1 caveat that flagged it as unresolved is superseded by this entry. Do not re-open it, re-derive it, or price a confirming pass against Google guidance.

Consequences, all unchanged by the ruling: the shell class keeps its 1 hard violator (commission-manifest.sh, 806) and 9 soft. The hard violator remains actionable for a reason that has nothing to do with the threshold debate - it embeds a 674-line Python program as a shell heredoc, which is a tooling and testability defect that would stand at any threshold.

summary: HITL: scope is a candidate 0.9.0 readability refactor, targeting BOTH human and agentic consumption
body:
HITL has placed this work as a potential 0.9.0 refactor whose goal is a level of readability for humans IN ADDITION TO agents. That dual audience is the governing constraint and it changes what "done" means.

The two audiences overlap but are not identical. Humans need topic boundaries, findability, and a chronological spine they can follow. Agents need bounded regions that fit a context window, stable anchors that survive edits, and no requirement to read 17,910 lines to answer a question about one capability. Where the two diverge, the divergence must be named rather than split the difference silently - the clearest instance already on record is STATUS-0.8.0.md at 2,087 lines (~32,000 tokens): the documentation literature says leave it intact, the context literature says it is already past the range where retrieval degrades. Recorded as a Phase 1 caveat; resolution is archive-and-link, not a split.

Scope consequence: 0.9.0 is NOT a splitting campaign. 59 of 66 flagged files are settled LEAVEs. The work is the engine decomposition, a small set of duplication and embedded-language defects, and a durable navigation layer.

summary: 0.9.0 readability refactor proposal written durably to dev/design/0.9.0-readability-refactor-proposal.md (status PROPOSED)
body:
The overall position now lives in a governed design record rather than only in session chat, per the standing rule that substantive positions go to the ledger and design records and chat only points at them.

THREE-PART POSITION.
1. This is NOT a splitting campaign. 59 of 66 flagged files are settled LEAVEs and the research says shortening them buys nothing. The deliverable is "the repo is navigable", not "the line counts came down" - different targets that a line-count framing conflates.
2. The engine IS the release. impl Engine is 5008 lines / 140 methods with a median method of 20 lines: one type doing 140 jobs. It obstructs both audiences at once - a human cannot hold 140 responsibilities, an agent cannot answer a one-capability question without ingesting 17,910 lines. Decomposition needs ZERO public API change (compiled, not argued). Gated on public-symbol baseline tooling that does not yet exist, and on a quiet window that 0.8.20 occupies.
3. The durable half is the navigation layer: structure maps, the advisory scanner, and this ledger of settled verdicts. The genuinely unresolved tension is STATUS-0.8.0.md - 2087 lines / ~32k tokens - where the documentation literature says leave it and the context literature says it is already past reliable retrieval. Archive-and-link resolves it, and is proposed as the pattern for every append-only record.

The doc also records what the review did NOT establish: no engine code was moved, no test run against a decomposed tree, the compile proof is narrow (it validates the mechanism, not the specific 20-module boundary), the thresholds are a convention with six of fifteen classes calibrated to this repo, three classes have no literature backing, and nothing has been sized for effort or risk.
